channel.title: Relational Tech Network Updates
channel.description: Meaningful changes across the relational tech ecosystem -- community tools, neighborhood apps, and civic technology.

item.title: cozy-corner: 5 commits by lovable-dev[bot]
item.description: Cozy Corner, the neighbor hub for 48th Ave in the Outer Sunset, now has an email reminder system set up and configured with sender and reply-to addresses. This means residents can receive timely reminders about local events and updates without having to check the site manually, making it easier to stay connected to neighborhood happenings. A small but meaningful step toward keeping a community loop active and reliable.

item.title: sunset-delib: Update
item.description: Welcome to the network, **sunset-delib**! We're thrilled to have this Relational Builder project join our growing community. Head over to their [repository](https://github.com/joshnesbit/sunset-delib) to check out what they're building!

item.title: New Haven Community Events Lending Library: Update
item.description: Welcome to the network, New Haven Community Events Lending Library! This wonderful project, stewarded by CWD and GROUP PROJECT, makes community gatherings more accessible by lending out chairs, PA systems, tents, lights, and more to New Haven neighbors. We're so glad to have you here and can't wait to see the events your resources help bring to life!
item.guid: welcome-new haven community events lending library

item.title: New Haven Community Events Lending Library: 11 commits by kaddae
item.description: The New Haven Community Events Lending Library got a round of meaningful updates, including copy improvements, a fix for a broken testimonials section, the ability for borrowers to specify how many items they need, and the addition of Civic Works and GROUP PROJECT logos in the footer with links to their sites. These changes make the platform clearer and more useful for community members looking to borrow event supplies, and they visibly connect the tool to the organizations stewarding it. Other builders running shared-resource or lending platforms might take note of the item quantity input as a simple but practical addition to request flows.

item.title: New Haven Community Events Lending Library: 10 commits by kaddae
item.description: The New Haven Community Events Lending Library got a round of visual and communication polish, including logo and branding refinements and a dedicated sending address for library emails. These changes help the tool feel more like a real, trustworthy institution in the community, and having emails come from a consistent address makes it easier for borrowers to recognize and respond to messages. Small details like these go a long way toward building trust with neighbors who are new to a community resource.

item.title: New-Sunset-App: Update
item.description: We're thrilled to welcome **New-Sunset-App** to the relational tech network! This project, built with Relational Builder, is a wonderful addition to our growing community of connected builders and creators. So glad to have you here, and we can't wait to see where this project goes!

item.title:
neighboring-recipes: Add BYOBallot to Civic Rhythms
Election-season living room gathering: friends and neighbors bring t
item.description: The neighboring-recipes cookbook now includes BYOBallot, a living room gathering practice where neighbors bring their ballots and share their voting reasoning in small rotating groups, contributed by Make Salem Awesome. This kind of structured, low-pressure civic conversation is hard to find recipes for, and having it documented in a forkable, freely licensed format means any neighborhood can adapt and try it. It's a good reminder that civic tech isn't always software.

item.title: cozy-corner: 7 commits by lovable-dev[bot]
item.description: Cozy Corner, the neighbor hub for 48th Ave in the Outer Sunset, got a fresh round of updates including new party stories, photos, and partner logos with acknowledgments. These additions help the site reflect the real community life happening on the block and give credit to the people and organizations making it possible. Other builders working on hyperlocal neighborhood hubs may find this a good model for documenting events and celebrating local partnerships.

item.title: Knowy: a neighborhood agent: 30 commits by joshnesbit
item.description: Knowy launched as a working neighborhood agent for the Outer Sunset, letting neighbors ask questions in plain language and get answers drawn from public neighborhood notes with cited sources. Every suggested change waits for a human steward to review before anything goes out, and neighbors can propose new data sources directly through the chat. Because the whole system is configured from a place's own notes, any community, whether a block, a co-op, or a neighborhood, can run their own version.

item.title: outer-sunset-today: 5 commits by lovable-dev[bot]
item.description: Outer Sunset Today added public feeds, making it possible for other tools and platforms to pull in community calendar data automatically. This opens the door for neighborhoods and builders to surface local events in their own apps, newsletters, or aggregators without manual copy-paste work. It's a meaningful step toward a more connected local information ecosystem.

item.title: Knowy: a neighborhood agent: Read outersunset.today's public pizza, school lunch, and news feeds
item.description: Knowy can now pull in live pizza menus, school lunch schedules, and neighborhood news from outersunset.today, so neighbors asking about food or local happenings get answers drawn from real, up-to-date public feeds. This matters because it shows how a neighborhood agent can connect to existing local data sources without requiring a private key or special access, keeping the whole setup transparent and easy to replicate. Builders running Knowy for their own place can use this same pattern to wire in whatever public feeds their neighborhood already publishes.

item.title: Knowy: a neighborhood agent: Make the home page clearer for first-time visitors
item.description: Knowy's home page now welcomes first-time visitors with clearer language about what the tool does and how it differs from a search engine or corporate chatbot. A quiet trust line surfaces key facts about privacy and sourcing right away, and also serves as the first visible path to the about and sources pages on a nav-free layout. Builders thinking about first impressions and trust-building for neighborhood AI tools will find the chip ordering and disappearing-on-scroll approach worth a close look.

item.title: Knowy: a neighborhood agent: README updated
item.description: Knowy now ships as a ready-to-remix template, with a blank data repo, a plain-language stewarding guide, and a half-page remix doc written for non-technical readers. This means any place, whether a house, a block, or a co-op, can stand up their own neighborhood agent without needing to reverse-engineer an existing deployment. Builders in this network can also use the new manifest format and commons intake doc as a reference for how to make their own projects forkable by neighbors.

item.title: Knowy: a neighborhood agent: Knowy as a template: manifest, blank notes, stewards' guide, remix page
item.description: Knowy, the neighborhood AI agent built for the Outer Sunset, is now packaged as a template that any community can copy and adapt for their own place, whether that's a block, a co-op, or a building. The release includes a blank data repo with placeholders, a plain-language guide to the human stewardship practice, and a half-page remix doc written for non-technical readers, so the barrier to running your own Knowy is documentation and community consent rather than figuring out the structure from scratch. Other builders in the network can now pick this up directly from the Builder commons.

item.title: Knowy: a neighborhood agent: Update
item.description: Welcome to the network, Knowy! 🎉 This Outer Sunset project reimagines what an AI agent can be by giving a *place* its own voice, answering neighbors' questions from shared notes while keeping humans in the loop as stewards of every change. We love seeing a tool built for collective care and local context, and can't wait to watch it grow.

item.title: The Sunset Wave: README updated
item.description: The Sunset Wave has published a full README explaining how their neighborhood host map works, how they protect host privacy, and how another community could adapt it for their own day of gatherings. This makes a lovely, working model for block-level coordination much easier to study and replicate. Builders in other neighborhoods now have a concrete starting point for running something similar on their own streets.

item.title:
The Sunset Wave: README: the story, what the map does, and how to make your own
Adds the two jobs the map does, wher
item.description: The Sunset Wave just published a full README explaining how their neighborhood gathering map works, how host privacy is protected, and how to adapt it for another neighborhood. This makes it possible for builders anywhere to pick up this model and run their own version, whether that's a day of block parties, a mutual aid network of hosts, or any event that benefits from a lightweight public map with privacy-conscious design. The addition of a .reltech.yml file also means the project is now discoverable across the Relational Tech Network.

item.title: Knowy: a neighborhood agent: README updated
item.description: Knowy now connects neighbors to each other, not just to what's already written down. A new 'Ask a Neighbor' feature lets someone send a question directly to a neighbor who offered to help, with privacy built in from the start: names and emails are kept in a separate contact store and never touch the shared notes, the index, or the AI's context. Other builders working on neighborhood knowledge tools will find a thoughtful model here for how to hold human connection alongside public information.

item.title: Knowy: a neighborhood agent: Ask a neighbor, and a commons for what the neighborhood knows
item.description: Knowy now connects neighbors to each other, not just to what the AI already knows. A new commons page shows neighborhood history, field notes, and a directory of neighbors who have offered to answer questions, and a new tool emails questions directly to those neighbors with their answer looped back through stewards into the shared notes. Privacy is built into the core: contact details never touch the data repo or the model, offers require email confirmation, and every relayed message includes a one-click stop link that deletes the contact immediately.

item.title: The Sunset Wave: Update
item.description: Welcome to the network, The Sunset Wave! This beautiful project is bringing neighbors together across 400 blocks of San Francisco's Sunset district for a single afternoon of community gatherings, hosted by the people who live there. We're so glad to have this kind of participatory, place-based work in the relational tech family.

item.title: Knowy: a neighborhood agent: Block by block: notes pinned to the map, and a lookup for one block
item.description: Knowy can now answer questions about a specific block or corner, drawing on notes pinned to the neighborhood map with sources, distances, and directions. This makes it possible for neighbors to ask what's historically or geographically special about their own stretch of street, and for other map tools to pull that same block story as open JSON. Any place running Knowy can add its own block notes, and places with none lose nothing.

item.title: Knowy: a neighborhood agent: Near me: an optional way to share the block you're on
item.description: Knowy now lets neighbors optionally share their block to get answers tailored to where they are, with two clear choices: just for this visit, or remembered on the device until turned off. The design is careful about privacy: only the block name and id are kept, the precise location point is never stored, and the feature stays off until a neighbor actively chooses it. Builders working on location-aware community tools will find a thoughtful model here for how to make 'near me' useful without accumulating sensitive data.

item.title: Knowy: a neighborhood agent: README updated
item.description: Knowy now lets neighbors ask about their specific block by name or corner, pulling together pinned notes, photographs, historical details, and nearby context without ever needing a street number or an outside mapping service. This means a place can build up a living, block-by-block memory of itself and share it through chat, a browsable page, or a JSON endpoint that other tools can use. An optional 'Use my location' button lets neighbors get answers tuned to where they are standing, with clear choices about how long that location is remembered.

item.title: Knowy: a neighborhood agent: Near me: one tap, and the browser's own prompt does the remembering
item.description: Knowy simplified how neighbors share their location when asking about nearby resources: now a single 'Use my location' link hands off to the browser's own permission prompt, letting the browser handle both consent and memory without the page asking its own separate questions. This removes a confusing double-prompt experience and puts neighbors in control using the privacy tools already built into their device. Other builders working on location-aware neighborhood tools will recognize this pattern as a cleaner way to respect consent without rolling custom permission flows.

item.title: Knowy: a neighborhood agent: Search: a good match comes first, whatever its source
item.description: Knowy's neighborhood search now ranks results by how well they match your question, not just by where they came from. Before this change, a weak match in a local history note could bury a strong recommendation or live business listing, so neighbors searching for a vet or a cafe were sometimes getting neighborhood history instead. Now the best answer rises to the top, whether it comes from block notes, curated recommendations, or live feeds.

item.title: The Sunset Wave: 4 commits by lovable-dev[bot]
item.description: The Sunset Wave has added a dedicated artist invitation flow to the site, including translated links in the footer, compensation details, and a private submission process where stewards can review work samples before they're shared more widely. This makes it easier for local artists to understand how they can contribute to the event and what they'll receive in return, with the translated footer link ensuring the invitation reaches neighbors across language backgrounds. Other builders working on community events with creative partnerships may find this lightweight steward-review model useful for handling submissions with care.

item.title: Knowy: a neighborhood agent: README updated
item.description: Knowy added a 'design brief' tool that helps builders understand what already exists in a neighborhood before starting something new: what's been asked for, who to talk to, what's nearby, and what data is available. This makes it easier for community builders to avoid duplicating work and to connect new ideas to real neighbors and existing resources from the very first step. The update also makes Knowy's core code fully reusable across any place, so a co-op, block, or neighborhood can run their own version without inheriting another community's name or credit.

item.title: Knowy: a neighborhood agent: Place pack: design brief, search by meaning, live endpoints
item.description: Knowy now exposes a set of tools that make it much easier for other builders to work alongside a neighborhood's agent: a new 'design brief' tool that takes a project idea and surfaces what already exists, who to talk to, upcoming events, and live data endpoints for that place. This means a builder starting something new for the Outer Sunset (or any place running their own Knowy) can get a grounded starting point from the neighborhood's own notes instead of beginning from scratch. The update also adds optional search by meaning, so neighbors and tools can find relevant records even when the exact words don't match, and it handles everything so that no information about who is searching gets sent anywhere.

item.title: Knowy: a neighborhood agent: Embed during the build, and show search status in place.json
item.description: Knowy now builds its semantic search index as part of the deployment process, so neighbors can search by meaning rather than just keywords from the moment the site goes live. This fixes a gap where the work of building the index could get dropped entirely on serverless hosts, leaving search less useful without any visible explanation. Stewards can now check a public status file to see whether meaning-based search is active, how many items are indexed, and what is preventing it if something is wrong.

item.title: The Sunset Wave: 5 commits by lovable-dev[bot]
item.description: The Sunset Wave has expanded its artist call form to include clearer guidance on submissions, optional links for additional work samples, and a submission deadline now displayed in all four supported languages. These updates make it easier for artists from across the neighborhood's diverse communities to understand what's expected and when to apply. The added bot protection also helps ensure that real neighbors are the ones finding their way into the host network.
